Probability and Statistics:
Counting: nPr = n!/(n-r)!, nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!).
Axioms: 0≤P(A)≤1, P(S)=1, P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A∩B).
Independence: P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). Mutually exclusive: P(A∩B)=0 (and generally NOT independent unless one has probability 0).
Conditional: P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B). Bayes: P(A|B)=P(B|A)P(A)/P(B).
E[X]=Σx·P(x) (discrete) or ∫x·f(x)dx (continuous). Var(X)=E[X²]-(E[X])². Conditional expectation E[X|Y=y] averages X over the conditional distribution.
Covariance: Cov(X,Y)=E[XY]-E[X]E[Y]. Correlation ρ=Cov(X,Y)/(σXσY), ρ∈[-1,1].
Bernoulli(p): mean=p, var=p(1-p). Binomial(n,p): mean=np, var=np(1-p). Uniform(a,b) continuous: mean=(a+b)/2, var=(b-a)²/12.
Exponential(λ): mean=1/λ, var=1/λ², memoryless property. Poisson(λ): mean=var=λ.
Normal(μ,σ²): 68-95-99.7 rule within 1/2/3 std devs. Standard normal Z=(X-μ)/σ. CDF F(x)=P(X≤x); PDF f(x)=dF/dx.
t-distribution: heavier tails than normal, used when population variance unknown and n small; converges to normal as df→∞.
Chi-squared: sum of squares of k independent standard normals; used in variance/goodness-of-fit tests.
Central Limit Theorem: sample mean of i.i.d. variables →Normal(μ, σ²/n) as n grows, regardless of population distribution.
Confidence interval (mean, known σ): x̄ ± z·(σ/√n). z-test: known variance. t-test: unknown variance/small n, df=n-1. Chi-squared test: goodness-of-fit / independence, statistic Σ(O-E)²/E.
Linear Algebra:
Vector space: closed under addition & scalar multiplication, must contain zero vector. Subspace: subset of a vector space that is itself a vector space.
Linear independence: c1v1+...+cnvn=0 only when all ci=0; else dependent.
Projection matrix P onto column space of A: P=A(AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀ; idempotent (P²=P) and symmetric.
Orthogonal matrix Q: QᵀQ=I, so Q⁻¹=Qᵀ; preserves lengths/angles.
Idempotent matrix: A²=A. Partition matrix: block form, multiply block-by-block matching dimensions.
Quadratic form xᵀAx: positive definite if all eigenvalues>0 (⇔ all leading principal minors >0).
Gaussian elimination: row-reduce [A|b] to echelon form to solve Ax=b or find rank.
Eigenvalues/eigenvectors: Av=λv ⇔ det(A-λI)=0. Trace(A)=Σλi. det(A)=Πλi. Symmetric real matrices → real eigenvalues, orthogonal eigenvectors.
Rank = number of linearly independent rows/columns = dimension of column space. Nullity = dim(null space). Rank-Nullity: rank(A)+nullity(A)=n (#columns).
Projection of b onto a: (aᵀb/aᵀa)·a.
LU decomposition: A=LU (L lower-triangular, U upper-triangular) via Gaussian elimination — speeds up solving Ax=b for multiple b.
SVD: A=UΣVᵀ, U/V orthogonal, Σ diagonal with singular values σi=√(eigenvalues of AᵀA), σi≥0, sorted descending.
Calculus and Optimization:
Limit: lim(x→a) f(x)=L means f(x)→L as x→a from both sides (must agree for limit to exist).
Continuity at a: lim(x→a)f(x)=f(a). Differentiability ⇒ continuity (not the reverse — e.g. |x| at 0).
Taylor series: f(x)=f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)+f''(a)(x-a)²/2!+... — local polynomial approximation.
Critical points: f'(x)=0 or undefined. Second-derivative test: f''>0 ⇒ local min, f''<0 ⇒ local max, f''=0 ⇒ inconclusive (check higher derivatives or sign change).
Single-variable optimization: check critical points AND domain endpoints/boundary for global max/min on a closed interval.
Common derivatives: d/dx[xⁿ]=nxⁿ⁻¹, d/dx[eˣ]=eˣ, d/dx[ln x]=1/x, d/dx[sin x]=cos x. L'Hôpital's rule for 0/0 or ∞/∞ limits: lim f/g = lim f'/g'.
Programming, Data Structures & Algorithm:
Stack: LIFO, push/pop O(1). Queue: FIFO, enqueue/dequeue O(1) (with proper implementation).
Linked list: O(1) insert/delete at known node, O(n) search. Tree: height h ⇒ up to 2^(h+1)-1 nodes (binary). BST search/insert/delete: O(h), O(log n) balanced, O(n) worst-case skewed.
Hash table: average O(1) insert/search/delete; O(n) worst case with collisions. Collision handling: chaining, open addressing (linear/quadratic probing).
Linear search: O(n). Binary search (sorted array): O(log n).
Selection sort: O(n²), always. Bubble sort: O(n²) worst/avg, O(n) best (already sorted, with early-exit flag). Insertion sort: O(n²) worst/avg, O(n) best — good for nearly-sorted data.
Merge sort: O(n log n) always, O(n) extra space, stable. Quicksort: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst (bad pivot choices), in-place, not stable.
Graph representations: adjacency matrix O(V²) space/O(1) edge lookup; adjacency list O(V+E) space, better for sparse graphs.
BFS: O(V+E), shortest path in unweighted graphs, uses a queue. DFS: O(V+E), uses a stack/recursion, good for cycle detection/topological sort.
Dijkstra's algorithm: shortest path with non-negative weights, O((V+E)log V) with a min-heap. Bellman-Ford: handles negative weights, O(VE), detects negative cycles.
Database Management & Warehousing:
ER model: entities, attributes, relationships; cardinality (1:1, 1:N, M:N).
Relational algebra ops: σ (select/filter rows), π (project/select columns), ⋈ (join), ∪/∩/− (set ops), × (Cartesian product).
Tuple calculus: {t | P(t)} — describes desired tuples via a predicate, not step-by-step operations (declarative, like SQL).
SQL: SELECT-FROM-WHERE-GROUP BY-HAVING-ORDER BY; JOIN types: INNER, LEFT/RIGHT/FULL OUTER.
Integrity constraints: primary key (unique, not null), foreign key (referential integrity), NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK.
Functional dependency X→Y: X determines Y. Candidate key: minimal superkey.
1NF: atomic (indivisible) attribute values, no repeating groups. 2NF: 1NF + no partial dependency of non-key attrs on part of a composite key. 3NF: 2NF + no transitive dependency (non-key attr depending on another non-key attr). BCNF: every determinant (LHS of every FD) is a superkey — strictly stronger than 3NF.
File organization: heap (unordered), sequential (sorted), hashed. Indexing: primary index (on ordering key), secondary index, B+ tree index — O(log n) search, common in DBs because it's disk-I/O-friendly.
Data transformation: normalization (scale features), discretization (continuous→categorical bins), sampling (subset selection), compression (reduce storage, e.g. run-length encoding).
Data warehouse: star schema = 1 fact table (measures) + denormalized dimension tables (fast queries, some redundancy). Snowflake schema = normalized dimension tables (less redundancy, more joins). Concept hierarchy: e.g. day→month→quarter→year, for OLAP roll-up/drill-down. OLAP measures: aggregated numeric facts (sum, count, avg) categorized by dimensions.
Machine Learning:
Simple/multiple linear regression: minimize Σ(y-ŷ)² (OLS); coefficients via normal equation β=(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy.
Ridge regression: adds λΣβ² penalty (L2) to OLS loss — shrinks coefficients, handles multicollinearity, never zeroes them out exactly.
Logistic regression: models P(y=1|x)=sigmoid(wᵀx+b)=1/(1+e^-(wᵀx+b)); decision boundary is linear in the log-odds.
k-NN: classify by majority vote (or average, for regression) of k nearest training points; no explicit training phase, sensitive to k and feature scaling.
Naive Bayes: assumes conditional independence of features given the class; P(class|x)∝P(class)·ΠP(xi|class).
LDA: assumes classes share a common covariance matrix, finds a linear projection maximizing between-class/within-class variance ratio; also usable for dimensionality reduction.
SVM: maximizes the margin between classes; support vectors are the closest points to the decision boundary; kernel trick handles non-linear boundaries.
Decision trees: split on the feature/threshold that most reduces impurity (Gini or entropy/information gain) at each node.
Bias-variance trade-off: high bias→underfitting (too simple), high variance→overfitting (too complex, fits noise). Total error ≈ bias² + variance + irreducible error.
Cross-validation: LOO (leave-one-out) trains on n-1 points, tests on 1, repeated n times — low bias, high variance, expensive. k-fold: split into k parts, train on k-1, test on 1, repeat k times, average — typical k=5 or 10.
Multi-layer perceptron / feedforward NN: layers of weighted sums + non-linear activation (sigmoid/ReLU/tanh); trained via backpropagation + gradient descent.
k-means: iteratively assign points to nearest of k centroids, then recompute centroids as cluster means; sensitive to initialization and k. k-medoid: like k-means but centers are actual data points (more robust to outliers).
Hierarchical clustering: agglomerative (bottom-up merge) or divisive (top-down split); linkage criteria — single (min distance), complete (max distance), average.
PCA: eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, ranked by eigenvalue (= variance explained along that direction); project data onto top-k components for dimensionality reduction.
Artificial Intelligence:
Uninformed search: BFS (complete, optimal for unit-cost edges, O(b^d) time/space), DFS (not optimal, less memory O(bd)), uniform-cost search (optimal for non-negative weighted edges).
Informed search: greedy best-first (uses heuristic h(n) only, not optimal in general), A* (uses f(n)=g(n)+h(n); optimal if h is admissible — never overestimates true cost — and consistent for graph search).
Adversarial search: minimax assumes optimal opponent, explores full game tree; alpha-beta pruning gives the same result as minimax while skipping branches that can't affect the decision.
Propositional logic: connectives ∧,∨,¬,→,↔; a sentence is valid if true in every model, satisfiable if true in some model, entails another sentence if the other is true whenever it is.
Predicate logic: adds quantifiers ∀ (for all), ∃ (there exists), predicates over objects, function symbols.
Reasoning under uncertainty: represent joint distributions compactly via conditional independence assumptions rather than full joint tables.
Conditional independence / Bayesian networks: DAG where each node is independent of its non-descendants given its parents; d-separation determines independence from graph structure.
Variable elimination (exact inference): sum out (marginalize) irrelevant variables one at a time from factors, in a chosen order, to compute a query's exact probability.
Approximate inference via sampling: generate samples consistent with (or reweighted for) evidence — e.g. rejection sampling, likelihood weighting, Gibbs sampling — trades exactness for scalability on large networks.
General Aptitude:
Verbal ability: read the full sentence before choosing — watch for subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, and modifier placement; for reading comprehension, answer from what the passage states, not outside knowledge.
Quantitative aptitude: percentages — a is what % of b = (a/b)×100. Ratios scale together. Time-speed-distance: distance=speed×time; relative speed adds (opposite directions) or subtracts (same direction). Time-and-work: rate = 1/(time to finish alone); combined rate = sum of individual rates.
Permutations/combinations basics: order matters → permutation (nPr); order doesn't → combination (nCr).
Analytical reasoning: for seating/arrangement puzzles, fix one entity as a reference point first; for blood relations, draw a quick family tree; for syllogisms, check whether a valid conclusion follows in ALL cases, not just the likely one; for series, check differences, ratios, or alternating patterns before giving up.
